title: Flu Season Arrives Weeks Early as Positive Tests Hit a 10-Year High for October; Texas Urges Shots Now
excerpt: Flu activity has been climbing since late August, with 5 percent of tests positive in the week ending Oct. 10 — a 10-year high for this point in the year — and Texas health officials are urging everyone 6 months and older to get a flu shot now.
content:
The 2026–27 flu season is off to an unusually early start. Flu activity in the United States has been rising since late August, and positive tests reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention hit 5 percent in the week ending Oct. 10 — a 10-year high for this time of year — according to Reuters. On the West Coast, the positivity rate reached 10.7 percent, compared with 0.5 percent a year earlier, and numbers are also elevated in eight Southern states.

CDC FluView data for the week ending Oct. 10 show 5.0 percent of clinical laboratory specimens tested positive for flu, up from 3.9 percent the week before. Influenza A(H1N1) accounted for 96.4 percent of the subtyped viruses reported by public health laboratories. Visits for flu-like illness reached 2.1 percent nationally, below the 2.9 percent national baseline, and the CDC had received no reports of pediatric flu deaths so far this season.

Physicians cited by Reuters are urging everyone 6 months and older to get vaccinated against the flu. The CDC’s outlook for the 2026–27 respiratory disease season expects the combined peak in hospitalizations from COVID-19, influenza and RSV to be similar to last season’s peak.

What Texas officials are saying

Oct. 2 was Texas Influenza Awareness Day, and the Texas Department of State Health Services (DSHS) is recommending early immunization as the new flu season begins. “We recommend everyone ages six months and older get a flu shot as soon as possible because we usually see cases start to rise at this time of year,” said DSHS Chief Medical Executive Manda Hall, MD. DSHS notes the body takes about two weeks to build flu antibodies after vaccination.

CDC data put flu-like illness at 2.1 percent of outpatient visits in Texas for the week ending Oct. 10 — the state’s highest reading so far this season and in line with the national average. DSHS says young children, older adults, pregnant women and people with chronic health conditions often suffer the most severe effects from flu, and that antiviral treatments are available but are most effective when started within 48 hours of symptoms beginning.

For Webb County families, the timing matters: with flu already climbing nationally weeks ahead of the usual November–December rise, state officials say the best time to get the shot is now, before holiday travel and gatherings begin.

Sources:

  • Reuters
  • Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — 2026–2027 Respiratory Disease Season Outlook
  • Texas Department of State Health Services news release
